content: Healthcare systems should prioritize the establishment of palliative care interdisciplinary teams (IDTs) in secondand third-level hospitals. These teams must include specialist physicians with intermediate-level training in palliative care. Generalist clinicians should receive basic palliative care training, which includes guidance on when and how to refer patients to higher-level IDTs. Some children experience refractory or complex symptoms that cannot be adequately managed by physicians with intermediate-level pediatric palliative care (PPC) training. These cases require intervention by palliative care specialist physicians who lead IDTs. However, there is a significant shortage of palliative care specialists in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), with even fewer PPC specialists and no dedicated PPC training programs. It is imperative to establish palliative care specialist training programs in LMICs as soon as possible. Ministries of health should formally recognize palliative medicine as a medical specialty to facilitate the development of these programs and enable their graduates to practice effectively. These training programs should include PPC training for all trainees and aim to develop a dedicated PPC specialist training track promptly. National healthcare policies should mandate that major children’s hospitals establish PPC services led by PPC specialist physicians within a specified timeframe. PPC specialists and IDTs are particularly critical in pediatric cancer centers, where many children with advanced cancer suffer from inadequately treated symptoms such as pain, dyspnea, and nausea/vomiting. Even in high-income countries, these symptoms are often poorly managed. Furthermore, new targeted cancer therapies and immunotherapies can exacerbate symptoms, create new ones, or lead to complex clinical dilemmas that require palliative care expertise. Similarly, hospitals offering invasive life-sustaining treatments, such as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), should provide palliative care services led by specialist physicians and IDTs. These services are essential to minimize the discomfort of critical care, offer alternatives to life-sustaining treatments of questionable benefit, and ensure the comfort of children for whom life-sustaining treatment will be withdrawn. The Essential Package of Pediatric Palliative Care and Symptom Relief (EP Ped) represents the minimum standard of palliative care and symptom relief that should be accessible to any child in any setting. This package includes safe, effective, inexpensive, off-patent, and widely available medicines, simple and affordable equipment, and basic social supports. Together, these resources can prevent and alleviate physical, psychological, social, and spiritual suffering. The package also includes the human resources necessary to apply these interventions appropriately, effectively, and safely, while supporting patients and families throughout the course of illness. The medicines included in the EP Ped are based on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for Children and are selected based on their necessity to address common symptoms and suffering in children with serious or life-threatening health conditions. Morphine, in oral fast-acting and injectable forms, is the most clinically important palliative care medicine. It must be accessible in appropriate forms and doses for patients with terminal dyspnea or moderate to severe pain, whether acute, chronic, or associated with malignancy. However, opioids should not be the first-line treatment for chronic non-malignant pain outside of cancer, palliative, or end-of-life care, except under special circumstances with strict monitoring. Oral morphine should be prioritized over injectable forms whenever clinically possible. All doctors caring for patients with moderate to severe pain or terminal dyspnea should be adequately trained and legally empowered to prescribe morphine in any necessary dose to provide adequate relief. Training in basic PPC, as outlined in this document, can prepare doctors inexperienced in prescribing morphine. Additionally, doctors should be able to prescribe sufficient supplies of morphine to minimize the need for frequent, burdensome travel for families. Non-opioid medicines, such as oral and injectable haloperidol and oral fluoxetine (or other SSRIs), are also essential in palliative care. Haloperidol is a first-line treatment for nausea, vomiting, agitation, delirium, and anxiety, while SSRIs like fluoxetine are first-line pharmacotherapy for depression or persistent anxiety in children older than eight years. Any doctor should be prepared and permitted to prescribe these medicines, not just psychiatrists or neurologists. Patients with severe psychiatric illnesses, such as psychotic or bipolar disorders, should be referred to specialist psychiatric care whenever possible. Petroleum jelly is essential for dressing non-healable wounds, as it prevents pain and bleeding associated with wet-to-dry dressings. Metronidazole powder, made by crushing metronidazole pills, is crucial for reducing or eliminating the odor of wounds infected with anaerobic bacteria. This powder can be applied directly to the wound or mixed with petroleum jelly or hydrogel dressings. The equipment included in the EP Ped must be necessary for relieving physical or psychological suffering, inexpensive, and simple to use with basic training. Examples include nasogastric tubes for refractory vomiting or medication administration, urinary catheters for bladder dysfunction, pressure-reducing mattresses to prevent and relieve pressure ulcers, locked safe-boxes for opioids, rechargeable flashlights for nocturnal home care, and diapers to reduce the risk of skin ulceration and infection. In countries where plastic bags are prohibited for environmental reasons, exceptions should be made for specialized medical use. Human resources and training requirements depend on the level and type of healthcare delivery site and the competency of staff in PPC. Any medical doctor, clinical officer, or assistant doctor trained in basic palliative care should be capable of preventing or relieving most pain and physical suffering. They should also be able to prescribe opioids like morphine and provide pharmacotherapy for uncomplicated anxiety disorders, depression, or delirium. Nurses, psychologists, social workers, and community health workers (CHWs) can be trained to provide culturally appropriate psychotherapy for depression and bereavement support. Nurse-anesthetists with basic palliative care training and nurse practitioners with advanced training may also provide these services in some settings.
